# Arginine vasopressin disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Fluids, electrolytes, and acid-base disorders > Arginine vasopressin disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/_T05t2)

---

## Summary

<u>Arginine vasopressin</u> (<u>AVP</u>) disorders are a group of conditions in which the <u>kidneys</u> cannot effectively concentrate urine, resulting in hypotonic <u>polyuria</u>. <u>Arginine vasopressin deficiency</u> (<u>AVP-D</u>), previously known as <u>central DI</u>, is the most common <u>AVP</u> disorder and is caused by decreased <u>hypothalamic</u> production or <u>pituitary</u> release of <u>AVP</u>, resulting in insufficient levels of circulating <u>AVP</u>. <u>AVP-D</u> can be primary (e.g., <u>idiopathic</u>, hereditary) or secondary (e.g., due to <u>brain lesions</u>, injury, infection). <u>Arginine vasopressin resistance</u> (<u>AVP-R</u>), previously known as <u>nephrogenic DI</u>, results from renal unresponsiveness to <u>AVP</u> and may be hereditary or acquired (e.g., medication-induced, renal disease). Most individuals with <u>AVP</u> disorders develop <u>polydipsia</u> and <u>polyuria</u> in response to excessive fluid loss. Individuals with <u>nocturia</u> may have <u>sleep deprivation</u> and/or daytime sleepiness. Children may present with nonspecific symptoms (e.g., irritability, <u>fever</u>), <u>clinical signs of significant dehydration</u>, and/or <u>clinical features of hypernatremia</u>. Initial diagnosis in adults is based on the presence of hypotonic <u>polyuria</u> on a <u>24-hour urine collection</u>. <u>Confirmatory testing</u> (e.g., <u>water deprivation test</u>) can differentiate between <u>AVP</u> disorders and <u>primary polydipsia</u>. Management includes oral fluids to compensate for urinary loss. For <u>AVP-D</u>, pharmacological therapy with <u>desmopressin</u> may be used; surgical intervention may be required for patients with <u>AVP-D</u> due to a <u>brain</u> mass. Management of acquired <u>AVP-R</u> involves treating the underlying cause; the condition is typically reversible within weeks to months, although <u>lithium</u>-induced <u>AVP-R</u> may be irreversible. Pharmacotherapy with <u>thiazide diuretics</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, or <u>amiloride</u> is indicated in some patients.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Arginine vasopressin deficiency</u> (<u>central diabetes insipidus</u>) [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)[[3]](/library/Yjdn_p0)




* Most common form: caused by insufficient or absent <u>hypothalamic</u> synthesis or <u>posterior pituitary</u> secretion of <u>AVP</u>

* Types

* Primary (∼ ⅓ of cases)

* Most cases are <u>idiopathic</u>.

* The hereditary form is rare.

* An autoimmune etiology of primary <u>AVP-D</u> has been suggested. [[4]](/library/_5Y55p)[[5]](/library/q_YC67)

* Secondary (∼ ⅔ of cases)

* <u>Brain tumors</u> (especially <u>craniopharyngioma</u>) and cerebral <u>metastasis</u> (most common: <u>lung cancer</u> and <u>leukemia</u>/<u>lymphoma</u>)

* Neurosurgery: usually after the removal of large <u>adenomas</u>

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u>, <u>pituitary</u> bleeding, <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Pituitary</u> <u>ischemia</u> (e.g., <u>Sheehan syndrome</u>, <u>ischemic stroke</u>)

* Infection (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>)

* Granulomatous disease affecting the <u>hypothalamus</u> (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>)

* Subtype: adipsic arginine vasopressin deficiency 

* <u>Hypothalamic</u> osmoreceptor defects lead to loss of thirst despite decreased <u>AVP</u> secretion.

* Associated with an increased risk of <u>hypernatremia</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>AVP-D</u> following neurosurgery is usually transient.




### <u>Arginine vasopressin resistance</u> (<u>nephrogenic diabetes insipidus</u>) [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)[[3]](/library/Yjdn_p0)




* Rare: caused by defective <u>AVP</u> <u>receptors</u> in the <u>distal</u> tubules and <u>collecting ducts</u>

* Types

* Hereditary (mutation in <u>AVP</u> <u>receptor</u>): very rare

* Acquired: typically reversible if the underlying cause is resolved

* Adverse effect of medications (<u>lithium</u>, <u>demeclocycline</u>)

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* Renal disease (e.g., <u>autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease</u>, <u>renal amyloidosis</u>, <u>obstructive uropathy</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>AVP</u> enables the integration of <u>aquaporins</u> into the plasma membrane of <u>collecting duct</u> cells → reabsorption of free water

* Either ↓ <u>AVP</u> (<u>AVP-D</u>) or defective renal <u>AVP</u> <u>receptors</u> (<u>AVP-R</u>) → impaired ability of the <u>kidneys</u> to concentrate urine (hypotonic <u>collecting ducts</u>) → dilute urine (low urine <u>osmolarity</u>)

* Hyperosmotic volume contraction [[6]](/library/I_YYp7)

* Loss of fluid with urine → increased <u>extracellular fluid</u> <u>osmolarity</u> → passage of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space → equalization of the osmolarities of the extracellular and intracellular fluid

* Due to the loss of fluid, the osmolarities of intracellular and extracellular compartments are now higher (hyperosmotic) than the initial values.

* The fluid volume is redistributed between the two compartments to equalize the osmolarities and remains lower than the initial values in each of them (volume contraction)





> [!NOTE]
> Note that in <u>AVP-D</u>, <u>AVP</u> levels are decreased, while in <u>AVP-R</u>, they are normal or increased to compensate for the high urine output.




![Volume-osmolarity (Darrow-Yannet) diagrams](media/vo9cndw0lfvhwqsl272fxzdm.jpg)

Volume-osmolarity (Darrow-Yannet) diagrams

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Polyuria</u> with dilute urine

* <u>Nocturia</u> → restless <u>sleep</u>, daytime sleepiness

* <u>Polydipsia</u> (excessive thirst)

* In cases of low water intake  → severe <u>dehydration</u> (<u>altered mental status</u>, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>coma</u>) and <u>hypotension</u>

* Symptoms may worsen during <u>pregnancy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> In the absence of <u>nocturia</u>, <u>AVP</u> disorders are very unlikely.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Obtain a thorough <u>patient history</u> and perform a <u>physical examination</u> to assess for possible <u>causes of AVP disorders</u>.

* Obtain initial studies including serum <u>sodium</u>, <u>plasma osmolality</u>, and <u>urine osmolality</u>.

* Obtain subsequent studies (e.g., <u>water deprivation test</u>) to distinguish between <u>primary polydipsia</u>, <u>AVP-D</u>, and <u>AVP-R</u>.

* See also “<u>Polyuria-polydipsia syndromes</u>” for expected laboratory findings.

* Obtain imaging to rule out <u>brain tumors</u> in patients with <u>AVP-D</u>.





![Diagnostic approach to suspected arginine vasopressin disorder (diabetes insipidus)](media/mkpninuylcjkf8ywnsxn7cqd.jpg)

Diagnostic approach to suspected arginine vasopressin disorder (diabetes insipidus)




### Initial <u>laboratory studies</u>  [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)[[7]](/library/iH1JJR0)




* Routine studies: <u>BMP</u>, <u>urinalysis</u>

* To rule out causes of <u>osmotic diuresis</u>, e.g., <u>hyperglycemia</u> with <u>glucosuria</u>

* To assess for acquired causes of <u>AVP-R</u>, e.g., <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>

* <u>24-hour urine collection</u>: to confirm hypotonic <u>polyuria</u>, i.e., urine volume > 50 mL/kg/24 hours with <u>urine osmolality</u> < 800 mOsm/kg

* Serum <u>sodium</u> and <u>plasma osmolality</u>

* ↓ Na<sup>+</sup> and/or ↓ <u>plasma osmolality</u>: <u>primary polydipsia</u> likely

* Normal values: Diagnosis is unclear; obtain subsequent studies to differentiate between <u>polyuria-polydipsia syndromes</u>.

* ↑ Na<sup>+</sup> and/or ↑ <u>plasma osmolality</u>: An <u>AVP</u> disorder is likely; obtain subsequent studies to differentiate between <u>AVP-D</u> and <u>AVP-R</u>.





### Subsequent <u>laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)[[7]](/library/iH1JJR0)[[8]](/library/sH1t7R0)




* To distinguish between <u>polyuria-polydipsia syndromes</u>, <u>AVP</u> activity can be assessed directly or indirectly.

* Consult <u>endocrinology</u> for guidance and follow local testing protocols if available.





#### Water deprivation test (indirect assessment of <u>AVP</u> activity)




Urine concentrating capacity is assessed during a period of <u>dehydration</u>; <u>desmopressin</u> is then administered to assess response to a synthetic <u>AVP analogue</u>. [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)




* Procedure

* Keep the patient <u>NPO</u>.

* Assess the following at baseline, then every 1–2 hours:

* Plasma <u>sodium</u> and <u>osmolality</u>

* Urine <u>sodium</u> and <u>osmolality</u>

* <u>Vital signs</u>

* Interpretation after period of water deprivation  [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)

* <u>Urine osmolality</u> increases to > 800 mOsm/kg: <u>Primary polydipsia</u> is confirmed.

* <u>Urine osmolality</u> remains ≤ 800 mOsm/kg: <u>AVP</u> disorders are likely ; administer <u>desmopressin</u> (a synthetic <u>AVP analogue</u>).

* Interpretation after <u>desmopressin</u> administration

* Initial <u>urine osmolality</u> 300–800 mOsm/kg and:

* Significant increase (≥ 10%) after <u>desmopressin</u>: partial <u>AVP-D</u>

* No or minimal increase (< 10%) after <u>desmopressin</u>: <u>primary polydipsia</u>

* Initial <u>urine osmolality</u> < 300 mOsm/kg and:

* Significant increase (> 50%) after <u>desmopressin</u>: complete <u>AVP-D</u> (indicating intact renal <u>AVP</u> <u>receptors</u>)

* No or moderate increase (< 50%) after <u>desmopressin</u>: <u>AVP-R</u> (indicating defective renal <u>AVP</u> <u>receptors</u>)





#### Plasma copeptin testing (direct assessment of <u>AVP</u> activity)  [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)[[8]](/library/sH1t7R0)




* Circulating plasma <u>copeptin</u> levels reflect circulating <u>AVP</u> levels.

* Measure random plasma <u>copeptin</u> levels.

* ≥ 21.4 pmol/L: <u>AVP-R</u> is confirmed.

* < 21.4 pmol/L: Obtain stimulated <u>plasma copeptin testing</u>, e.g., hypertonic saline infusion test. 

* > 4.9 pmol/L: <u>primary polydipsia</u>

* ≤ 4.9 pmol/L: <u>AVP-D</u>





> [!TIP]
> Plasma <u>AVP</u> measurement is not routinely utilized because results are unreliable, as <u>AVP</u> is unstable and has a short <u>half-life</u> ex vivo.




### <u>Brain</u> imaging [[7]](/library/iH1JJR0)[[9]](/library/PH1WqR0)




* Indications: suspected or confirmed <u>AVP-D</u> to determine the underlying cause

* Preferred modality: <u>pituitary</u> or <u>sella</u> protocol <u>MRI</u>

* Supportive findings: may reveal a <u>tumor</u>, inflammation, or infiltrative changes in the <u>posterior pituitary gland</u>





![Craniopharyngioma](media/yq01dtqqwtdrkoqh36qebi26.jpg)

Craniopharyngioma

### Other causes of <u>polyuria</u> and/or <u>polydipsia</u>




* Untreated <u>diabetes mellitus</u>

* Other causes of <u>osmotic diuresis</u>

* Beer potomania: dilutional <u>hyponatremia</u> secondary to limited renal free water excretion caused by intake of large amounts of beer  [[10]](/library/DL01-g)





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

The goals of management are to reduce <u>polyuria</u> and <u>polydipsia</u> to improve the patient's quality of life and maintain <u>eunatremia</u>.




### General principles [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)




* Encourage adequate fluid intake and a low-<u>sodium</u>, low-protein diet.

* Initiate <u>management of hypernatremia</u> (i.e., <u>replace free water deficit</u>) as needed.

* Treat according to the underlying mechanism and cause.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Hypernatremia</u> is rare in the ambulatory setting but may be present in patients with cognitive impairment, <u>adipsic</u> <u>AVP-D</u>, and those who are hospitalized or cannot access water because of mobility impairment. [[11]](/library/Ys1ntR0)




### <u>Arginine vasopressin deficiency</u> [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)




* Management should be guided by an endocrinologist.

* Most patients are able to maintain <u>eunatremia</u> through increased oral fluid intake alone.

* Initiate pharmacotherapy in patients with either:

* <u>Polyuria</u> and/or <u>polydipsia</u>

* <u>Hypernatremia</u>

* Agents

* <u>Desmopressin</u> (preferred): synthetic <u>AVP analogue</u> without vasoconstrictive effects 

* Intranasal administration is preferred.

* Typically at bedtime to relieve <u>nocturia</u>

* Start at a low dose to reduce the risk of overcorrection.

* <u>Chlorpropamide</u> (alternative): enhances the effect of <u>AVP</u> and increases its secretion





> [!TIP]
> Most patients with <u>AVP-D</u> are able to increase their oral fluid intake to maintain <u>eunatremia</u> without pharmacotherapy. However, <u>desmopressin</u> is typically required to relieve bothersome symptoms of <u>polyuria</u> and <u>polydipsia</u>. [[7]](/library/iH1JJR0)




### <u>Arginine vasopressin resistance</u> [[2]](/library/GH1B7R0)




* Consult nephrology as needed for guidance on management.

* Treat the underlying cause, if applicable, e.g.:

* Discontinue the causative agent (e.g., <u>lithium</u>, <u>demeclocycline</u>).

* <u>Correct electrolyte imbalances</u> (e.g., <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>).

* Relieve <u>urinary tract obstruction</u>.

* Consider pharmacotherapy to manage <u>polyuria</u> and <u>hypernatremia</u>.

* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u>

* Lead to <u>sodium</u> depletion, which increases <u>sodium</u> and water reabsorption in the <u>proximal</u> tubules

* As a result, less water reaches the <u>distal</u> collecting tubules and urine volume decreases

* <u>NSAIDs</u> (e.g., <u>indomethacin</u>)

* <u>Amiloride</u>: indicated in patients with <u>lithium</u>-induced <u>AVP-R</u> who continue <u>lithium</u> therapy





> [!WARNING]
> In patients with renal disease, <u>NSAIDs</u> must be used with caution because of the potential <u>nephrotoxic</u> effects.

---

## Special patient groups

### <u>Gestational AVP disorder</u> (gestational diabetes insipidus) [[12]](/library/qo1C130)




* Definition: transient <u>AVP</u> disorder caused by increased activity and/or circulating levels of vasopressinase during <u>pregnancy</u> that typically resolves after delivery

* Etiology: decreased metabolization of <u>vasopressinase</u> due to impairment in <u>hepatic function</u>  (e.g., due to <u>HELLP</u>, <u>AFLP</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>)

* Pathophysiology

* ↓ <u>Peripheral vascular resistance</u> and blood pressure → ↓ threshold for <u>AVP</u> secretion.

* ↑ <u>Vasopressinase</u> secretion from <u>placental</u> <u>trophoblasts</u> after 8 weeks' <u>gestation</u>

* ↑ Compensatory <u>AVP</u> production

* Clinical features: same as in nonpregnant individuals

* Diagnostics 

* <u>24-hour urine collection</u> to confirm <u>polyuria</u> (urine output > 3 L/day)

* <u>Desmopressin</u> challenge test

* Treatment: <u>desmopressin</u>

* Complications: <u>preeclampsia</u>, <u>oligohydramnios</u>





### AVP disorders in children [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)[[13]](/library/gCdFrH0)[[14]](/library/TCd6rH0)




#### Etiology [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)




The <u>etiology of AVP disorders</u> in children is similar to that in adults.




* <u>AVP-D</u> is most common (∼90% of cases); <u>AVP-R</u> is rare. [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* Secondary causes are more common and include:

* Congenital causes (e.g., <u>septo-optic dysplasia</u>, <u>holoprosencephaly</u>)

* Acquired causes (same as those in adults; see “<u>Etiology of AVP disorders</u>”)

* Hereditary causes are rare (mostly X-linked <u>AVP</u>-<u>receptor</u> mutations).





#### Clinical features [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)[[13]](/library/gCdFrH0)




* The age of onset depends on the underlying cause.  [[13]](/library/gCdFrH0)

* <u>Clinical features of AVP disorders</u> are similar in adults and children.

* Additional manifestations in <u>infants</u> and children include: [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)[[13]](/library/gCdFrH0)

* Cold water cravings

* Primary or <u>secondary enuresis</u>

* <u>Fever</u>

* Irritability

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Vomiting</u>

* <u>Constipation</u>

* <u>Growth faltering</u>  [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* Manifestations suggestive of secondary <u>AVP-D</u> include: [[13]](/library/gCdFrH0)

* <u>Brain tumor</u>: visual defect, <u>diplopia</u>, <u>precocious puberty</u>

* <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>: <u>rash</u>, recurrent <u>otitis media</u>, bone <u>pain</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Children with <u>AVP</u> disorders, especially if nonverbal and/or <u>adipsic</u>, are at high risk for <u>hypernatremic</u> <u>dehydration</u>. [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)




#### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)




* Obtain <u>24-hour urine collection</u> to confirm hypotonic <u>polyuria</u>. 

* <u>Polyuria</u> in children:

* <u>Neonates</u>: > 150 mL/kg/day [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* <u>Infants</u> and children aged ≤ 2 years: > 100–110 mL/kg/day [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* Older children: > 40–50 mL/kg/day [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* <u>Urine osmolality</u> < 300 mOsm/kg and <u>serum osmolality</u> > 300 mOsm/kg suggests an <u>AVP</u> disorder. [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)

* Obtain <u>BMP</u> to:

* Assess for <u>hypernatremia</u>  [[15]](/library/XBd9zH0)

* Exclude mimics of <u>AVP</u> disorders (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>)

* Assess for causes of acquired <u>AVP-R</u> (e.g., <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>)

* Findings suggestive of an <u>AVP</u> disorder: Refer to pediatric <u>endocrinology</u> for further diagnostics, including 

* <u>Water deprivation test</u>

* Evaluation for an underlying etiology (e.g., <u>brain</u> imaging, <u>tumor markers</u>, <u>genetic testing</u>)





#### Management [[1]](/library/2CdTrH0)[[14]](/library/TCd6rH0)




* Refer to a pediatric specialist (e.g, endocrinologist or nephrologist) for management.

* Provide the following dietary recommendations:

* Free access to water

* <u>Low-sodium diet</u>

* Adequate caloric intake (specialist consultation is recommended)  [[14]](/library/TCd6rH0)

* Specialist treatment may include:

* Management of reversible causes (e.g., <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>obstructive uropathy</u>)

* Pharmacologic therapy (e.g., <u>desmopressin</u>, <u>thiazide diuretics</u>, <u>NSAIDs</u>, and/or <u>amiloride</u>)

---
